UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND  
PROTEST OF TALEN ENERGY CORPORATION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and 
Large Load Registry to Address System Reliability1 proposal should be rejected because it is 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.  While Talen appreciates PJM’s goals of 
protecting ratepayers from rising costs while maintaining reliability, the vehicle chosen by PJM to 
arrive at that destination is a lemon and, as explained in the attached testimony of Zachary Ming 
of Energy and Environmental Economics, Inc. (“E3”), will result in inaccurate price signals, early 
and unnecessary generation resource retirements, and increased prices in the long-term.  First and 
foremost, however, PJM’s vehicle should not even be on the road because it does not comply with 
well-established law. 
The IRAS Proposal fails to comply with PJM’s Operating Agreement and the Federal 
Power Act (“FPA”).2  PJM claims that New Large Load is not similarly situated to other load, 
including existing Large Load, and thus is not unduly discriminated against under the IRAS 
Proposal.  PJM’s argument is erroneous and conclusory.  PJM cannot explain how New Large 
Load is uniquely situated in the context of procuring new capacity and emergency curtailment.  In

fact, PJM’s Operating Agreement requires the grid operator to apply emergency procedures “to all 
Members on a non-discriminatory basis.”3  The IRAS Proposal, contrary to the Operating 
Agreement, singles out New Large Load for curtailment during NERC Emergency Energy Alert 
Level 1 (“EEA1”) periods even before Demand Resources that have previously agreed to curtail.4   
PJM’s claim that the States retain “exclusive jurisdiction” to determine which specific New 
Large Load customers will be curtailed is also unavailing.5  PJM proposes to single out which 
customers to curtail but leave the final “flip the switch” decision to the States.  A State is not truly 
exercising its “exclusive jurisdiction” if the only decision it is left with is to take the action PJM 
directs or not act at all.  In effect, PJM is creating an unduly discriminatory tariff regime that 
unlawfully encroaches on the States’ exclusive jurisdiction.  This is patently unjust and 
unreasonable. 
The IRAS Proposal does not make economic sense either and will not result in the long-
term stability that PJM is seeking.  Zachary Ming of E3 explains in his attached testimony that the 
IRAS Proposal will have “knock-on effects” resulting in uneconomic outcomes and diminished 
reliability in the long-term.6  Specifically, excluding New Large Load7 from the Variable Resource 
Requirement (“VRR”) Curve artificially limits competition in the existing capacity market.8  The 
result will initially be a capacity clearing price that fails to equal net Cost of New Entry (“CONE”),

paradoxical result of PJM’s IRAS Proposal will be increased societal costs and decreased system

Talen Energy Corporation (“Talen”) agrees that PJM capacity market reform is necessary.  
The IRAS Proposal is just not the solution.  PJM conducted several Critical Issue Fast Path 
processes over the past year to address capacity shortfalls and large load demand.  The result of 
that effort were dozens of rejected proposals, including eleven proposals related to PJM’s “connect 
and manage” construct—the predecessor to IRAS.10  PJM’s Board eventually overruled the 
stakeholders’ rejections and moved forward with the rebranded “IRAS” Proposal nonetheless.11 
Talen supports holistic market reform that is non-discriminatory, legally durable, and 
methodical, with short-term and long-term implications in mind.  Such holistic reform should focus 
on increasing supply in the PJM region by incentivizing new generation resources to come online 
inside the existing reliability pricing model (“RPM”) structure.  The IRAS Proposal is premature 
and permanent and should not be adopted because it will circumvent much needed holistic 
reform.12  Talen respectfully submits this protest (“Protest”) to the IRAS Proposal accordingly13

I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,14 Talen 
respectfully submits this motion to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding.  The formal legal 
name of Talen is Talen Energy Corporation.  Talen is a corporation organized and existing under 
the laws of Delaware.  Talen maintains its principal place of business at 2929 Allen Parkway, 22nd 
Floor, Houston, Texas 77019. Talen is a leading independent power producer and energy 
infrastructure company which owns and operates approximately 15.7 gigawatts of power 
infrastructure in the United States.  Talen produces and sells electricity, capacity, and ancillary 
services into wholesale U.S. power markets, including and primarily in PJM.  Accordingly, the 
actions taken by the Commission in this matter will directly affect the interests of Talen.  Talen 
has a direct and material interest in the instant proceeding that no other party can adequately 
represent.  Talen therefore requests that the Commission grant this motion to intervene and permit 
Talen to participate in this proceeding with full rights as a party thereto. 
II. 
PROTEST 
The existing RPM construct was designed to improve price stability, enhance reliability, 
and produce accurate price signals to incentivize new generation build.15  The U.S. Supreme Court 
observed that  
[t]he capacity auction serves to identify the need for new generation:  
A high clearing price in the capacity auction encourages new 
generators to enter the market, increasing supply and thereby 
lowering the clearing price in the same-day and next-day auctions 
 
14  18 C.F.R. § 385.214.  
15  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 117 FERC ¶ 61,331 at PP 68-69 (2006) (internal citation omitted).

5 
 
three years’ hence; a low clearing price discourages new entry and 
encourages retirement of existing high-cost generators.16   
PJM has adapted its approach to capacity auctions over past decades to produce more accurate and 
defined price signals.  For example, PJM’s historical Capacity Credit Market (“CCM”) was 
replaced by the reliability pricing model (“RPM”) twenty years ago because the CCM did “not 
enable market participants to see the reliability problems in particular locations” and did “not 
provide price signals that would elicit solutions to reliability problems in enough time before the 
problem occurs. . . .”17  If the goal is to produce accurate price signals that send clear messages to 
new generation to build or to existing and costly generation to retire, then the market—a simulated 
competitive construct—cannot perform efficiently if PJM interferes with the capacity auctions by 
implementing artificial caps on supply and demand.  Yet, that is the imprudent design and purpose 
of the IRAS Proposal.      
A. 
PJM’s proposal to require New Large Loads to procure new capacity or be 
subject to curtailment is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, and 
unlawfully encroaches on State jurisdiction.  
Section 205(b) of the FPA prohibits the Commission from approving unjust, unreasonable, 
and unduly discriminatory tariffs.18  The regulated utility, as the movant under FPA Section 205, 
carries the burden of proof that its proposal is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory 
“[b]ecause a regulated utility is the party with access to the necessary information [and] bears the 
risk of an undeveloped or inconclusive record.”19 “Discrimination is undue when there is a 
 
16  Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., 136 S. Ct. 1288, 1293 (2016). 
17  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 117 FERC ¶ 61,331 at P 20. 
18  16 U.S.C. § 824d(b). 
19  Nantahala Power & Light Co. v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1342, 1351 (4th Cir. 1984); 16 U.S.C. § 824d.

6 
 
difference in rates or services among similarly situated customers that is not justified by some 
legitimate factor.”20   
The Commission has explained that similarly situated does not mean that customers must 
be without difference.21  Rather, “it means that there are no differences that are material to the 
inquiry at hand.”22  The Commission has also held that “entities are similarly situated if they are 
in the same position with respect to the ends that the law seeks to promote or the abuses that it 
seeks to prevent, even if they are different in many other respects.”23  For example, in Calpine 
Oneta Power, L.P.,24 the Commission held that new and existing generators were similarly situated 
for purposes of providing reactive power because they were equally capable of providing that 
service.25  In Iberdrola Renewables, Inc. v. Bonneville Power Admin.,26 the Commission held that 
“non-[f]ederal resources are similarly situated to [f]ederal hydroelectric and thermal resources for 
purposes of transmission curtailments because they all take firm transmission service.”27 
The purpose of the IRAS Filing is to address a capacity shortfall, which means procuring 
new capacity and curtailing load during emergency events.  Most load can procure new capacity 
prior to and after commencing service.  Moreover, requiring curtailment of New Large Load in the

broad sense fails to take into consideration both that not all New Large Load is so flexible and that 
certain load other than New Large Load is also capable of electing to curtail.  PJM’s proposed 
disparate treatment of New Large Load is therefore unjust, unreasonable, and unduly 
discriminatory. 
1. 
PJM’s requirement that only New Large Load execute contracts with 
BYONC resources or be subject to curtailment is unjust, unreasonable, and 
unduly discriminatory. 
PJM is only requiring New Large Load to contract with BYONC resources to avoid 
curtailment.  PJM does not dispute this disparate treatment.  Instead, PJM attempts to argue that 
New Large Load is not similarly situated to any other load.  What PJM means is that the IRAS 
Proposal admittedly discriminates against New Large Load, but PJM does not believe it is “undue” 
discrimination.  PJM is mistaken.  The evidence presented by PJM to justify its argument is limited 
to two statements:  (1) members of Congress have said that it would not be unduly discriminatory 
to treat data centers differently given their “incomparably large energy demands, how quickly data 
centers can come online, and their unique potential to impact the reliability of the electric grid”;28 
and (2) an out-of-context statement by the Commission  that “large loads constitute ‘a separate 
category of load’ because of their “size, operational behavior, and unique potential to impact the 
transmission system.”29  However, these are mere differences in customer profiles and cannot 
support a finding of differences “that are material to the inquiry at hand.”30  The inquiry at hand is

are/publicdisclosures/2025/20251106-congressional-letter-re-cifp-lla.pdf [https://perma.cc/ZKA9-Q5LZ]).

2026 Order”)).

which loads are capable of bringing their own new capacity and which loads are capable of electing 
to curtail in emergency events.   
Nearly all new commercial load is capable of procuring new capacity.  PJM does not limit 
bilateral capacity markets to specific customers, nor does PJM limit capacity transactions to only 
large loads.  In fact, PJM’s Capacity Exchange system allows unit-specific bilateral transactions 
of as little as 0.1 MW.31  This means that New Large Load, existing Large Load, new commercial 
load, and others are “in the same position with respect to the ends that” the IRAS Proposal “seeks 
to promote.”32     
Resources beyond just New Large Load are also capable of electing to curtail service 
during emergency events, e.g., large commercial industrial customers and existing Large Load.  
Existing Large Load is completely indistinguishable from New Large Load in this context, just as 
new and existing generation resources were equally capable of providing reactive power service 
in Calpine.33  This is also similar to federal and non-federal generation resources being equally 
able to curtail transmission service in Iberdrola.34  Although the customers at issue in Iberdrola 
were all taking firm transmission service, the only reason New Large Load would be taking a 
different service here, i.e., IRAS, is because PJM would force them to do so.   
PJM attempts to build its argument for discriminating against New Large Load based on 
prior Commission language from the recent series of show cause orders issued to the six regional

grid operators.35  Although the Commission proposed a definition for large load in the show cause 
orders, the Commission was not implying that discriminating against such large load was just and 
reasonable.  Moreover, the broad definition of large load that the Commission used in the show 
cause orders is not applicable to the inquiry at hand in this proceeding.  Even the Commission 
recognized in the show cause orders that only “flexible large loads that are willing and able to limit 
their use of the transmission system under certain conditions” should be offered a different 
transmission service.36  The Commission clarified that “‘flexible’ large loads are a subset of large 
loads, as used in [that] order, that are not co-located with generation, but are willing and able to 
limit their energy withdrawals from the transmission system under certain conditions.”37  
Therefore, PJM’s reliance on the Commission’s recent show cause orders to discriminate against 
New Large Loads is misplaced. 
2. 
Certain features of the IRAS Proposal are also unjust and unreasonable 
due to PJM’s arbitrary and disparate treatment of load. 
a. 
The IRAS Proposal arbitrarily sets an unsupported floor for New 
Large Load. 
The size of a particular load is irrelevant to an inquiry regarding which entities can curtail.  
Nonetheless, the IRAS Proposal sets a 50 MW floor for New Large Load.  PJM has not provided 
any justification for this disparate treatment of load, nor can it.   
Take an electric arc furnace facility (steel plant) in Pennsylvania for example.  Electric arc 
furnaces are now the predominant method for steel production in the country and consume 40-200

MW of electricity.38  Steel mills can temporarily shut down if needed during power shortages.39  
Under the IRAS Proposal, a 50 MW electric arc furnace would be curtailed first as a New Large 
Load, even though a 40 MW electric arc furnace in the same region could similarly reduce its 
respective load (and be compensated by PJM for doing so).  There is no difference between these 
customers with respect to the inquiry at hand.  In fact, they are equally capable of providing the 
ends that PJM seeks.  Accordingly, PJM’s disparate treatment of New Large Load under the IRAS 
Proposal is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory. 
b. 
The IRAS Proposal provides PJM with unjust, unreasonable, and 
unfettered discretion to issue curtailment directives. 
Well-established Commission precedent provides that matters directly affecting rates must 
be included in an RTO’s filed tariff if the matter “significantly affects rates, terms, and conditions” 
of service, are readily susceptible of specification, and not generally understood in a contractual 
agreement.40  The IRAS Proposal provides that PJM will determine a quantity of MW that load in 
a zone/area needs to curtail to maintain system reliability and will instruct the Electric Distributor

11 
 
to curtail such MW quantity, which will be equal to or less than the Eligible New Large Load 
Amount.41  The IRAS Proposal is silent, however, with respect to how PJM will determine the 
MW quantity to be curtailed or which Electric Distributors will be instructed to curtail.  The ability 
to curtail load and the potential to receive IRAS payments for such action certainly and 
significantly affects the rates, terms, and conditions of IRAS.  PJM must also have a process that 
is capable of being translated in written form to make such determinations and include those 
determinations in its Tariff.  Moreover, this proposal is a novel construct introduced for the first 
time by PJM and is not generally understood under traditional Tariff contractual arrangements.  
Therefore, under FERC’s “rule of reason” doctrine, PJM must include specific language regarding 
how it will determine the MW quantity to be curtailed and which Electric Distributors it will 
instruct to do so.  The potential for arbitrary and capricious decision-making in PJM’s process is 
too great to move forward without such specification.  Load being served under IRAS cannot make 
informed commercial decisions if it must read tea leaves to determine when and how much it will 
be curtailed in a region-wide reliability event. 
PJM carries the burden to prove that the IRAS Proposal is just and reasonable.42  The 
economic reality of the IRAS Proposal is that it will result in inaccurate price signals, early and 
unnecessary generation retirements, increased prices in the long term, and its implementation will 
be left to an opaque process known only to PJM.  The Commission cannot find such results to be 
just and reasonable and thus must reject the IRAS Proposal. 
 
41  IRAS Proposal at 86-87 (defining Eligible New Large Load Amount as “the MW value of load that an Eligible 
New Large Load in a given zone/area may be required to be made available to IRAS.”).

c. 
The IRAS proposal fails to account for New Large Load that 
previously contracted for capacity from existing resources. 
Chairman Laura Swett assured stakeholders that the Commission’s actions with respect to 
large load reforms and procedures “are not intended to disrupt existing commercial agreements.”43  
Talen has previously explained that PJM’s reliability backstop procurement (“RBP”) proposal 
would result in such load paying incremental capacity charges under the RBP.44  This is harmful 
to the entire market because “uncertainties regarding rate stability and contract sanctity can have 
a chilling effect on investments and a seller’s willingness to enter into long-term contracts and this, 
in turn, can harm customers in the long run.”45  PJM is inserting additional uncertainty into the 
market through the forced interruption of service to certain New Large Loads that are not allocated 
RBP capacity and costs.  Accordingly, the IRAS Proposal fails to even treat New Large Load on 
a consistent basis and unjustly introduces a chilling effect on investments in PJM.   
3. 
PJM’s directive to curtail New Large Load unlawfully commandeers the 
States’ exclusive jurisdiction. 
The FPA properly establishes the Commission’s jurisdiction over wholesale activity, while 
States retain their exclusive jurisdiction to regulate retail transactions.46  The FPA follows the 
Tenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, which provides that “[t]he powers not delegated to 
the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States

events/events/june-18-2026-open-meeting-10082025. 
44  Motion to Intervene and Request for Clarification of Talen Energy Corporation, Docket No. EC26-3380-000 
(filed Aug. 21, 2026).

would indirectly impact retail rates or State regulatory practices.  Such is an inevitability in an 
industry subject to multiple jurisdictions.  However, there are limits on the Commission’s ability 
to impact State practices. 
The U.S. Supreme Court has clarified the “anti-commandeering doctrine” over years of 
precedent.  Most pertinent here, in New York v. United States,48 the Court held that “Congress may 
not commandeer the States’ legislative processes by directly compelling them to enact and enforce 
a federal regulatory program . . . .”49  In that case, Congress passed a law requiring States to either 
establish nuclear waste disposal sites or, if a State chose not to establish such waste sites, the State 
would be required to take title to the waste and be liable for any damage to the generator or owner 
as a result of the State’s failure to take prompt possession.  The option to establish waste sites was 
encouraged through monetary incentives.  The Court held that this choice “would effectively 
‘commandeer’ States into the service of federal regulatory purposes” and in reality “the States’ 
‘choice’ is no choice at all.”50 
The IRAS Proposal similarly leaves States with no “choice.”  PJM claims that its proposal 
does not infringe on States’ exclusive jurisdiction because the decision “rests with the [S]tates to 
ensure that the appropriate retail customers, i.e., New Large Loads, including data centers—and 
not residential customers or small industrial customers—are reduced when system conditions call

for PJM to require load reductions according to IRAS.”51  However, PJM also explains that the 
entities directing load reductions “will be guided by the Large Load Registry.”52  In other words, 
PJM will provide the incentive and tools to curtail a specific class of customers, but argues that its 
hands are clean because it does not make the ultimate decision.  The ultimate decision is left to 
States, LSEs, and Electric Distributors or, if these entities do not act accordingly, residential 
customers and other small industrial load will bear additional costs in a manner inconsistent with 
cost causation principles.  This is not a “choice” at all.  Rather, PJM has commandeered State 
regulatory constructs and entities to implement its IRAS Proposal.  Such a result cannot stand 
under the Constitution and well-established precedent. 
PJM relies heavily on the Ratepayer Protection Pledge53 and the Statement of Principles 
Regarding PJM, which was signed by 13 governors of the PJM States, to justify the IRAS 
Proposal.54  Notwithstanding PJM’s reliance on these sources, they do not supersede the 
Constitution.  Even if the governors of each State publicly supported the IRAS Proposal, the IRAS 
Proposal would still run afoul of the anti-commandeering doctrine.  The Court in New York v. 
United States explained there that New York officials’ support of the legislation was irrelevant 
because “[t]he Constitution does not protect the sovereignty of States for the benefit of States or 
state governments . . . [t]o the contrary, the Constitute divides authority between federal and state

PJM’s argument cannot find refuge under EPSA either.57  The Court in that case held that 
the Commission’s regulation of demand response as permissible because it only addressed

even acknowledges that the implementation of the compensation scheme under IRAS “relies on 
application of state retail law.”60 Any one of these issues is fatal to the legality of the IRAS

B. 
Even if the IRAS Proposal stood on solid legal ground—which it does not—
the proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it will ultimately result in 
increased costs and could lead to further unduly discriminatory behavior. 
It is a well-accepted economic principle that competitive markets result in fair prices for 
goods, incentivize innovation, and encourage overall market efficiency, as further described in the 
attached Affidavit of Zachary Ming.61  Such markets, however, are difficult to develop organically 
in industries with high cost of entry.  Governmental or quasi-governmental organizations may 
design and oversee regulated markets under operational parameters that the regulators believe 
would simulate the results that a competitive market would produce.  PJM’s capacity market is a 
prime example of such a simulated market.  The simulated market results will inevitably start to 
diverge from true competitive market outcomes as more artificial interference is introduced to the 
market design.  The IRAS Proposal and its ultimate impact on PJM’s capacity market is no
